Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ be a **closed** complex contour, that is a
rectifiable path with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$
([[def-complex-contours-reversal-concatenation-and-closedness]]), with trace
$\gamma^\ast$, and let $p\in\mathbb C$ with $p\notin\gamma^\ast$. The **winding
number**, or **index**, of $\gamma$ about $p$ is

$$n(\gamma,p):=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\gamma\frac{dz}{z-p},$$

the complex line integral of
[[def-complex-line-integral-over-a-rectifiable-path]].

The integral exists: $z\mapsto1/(z-p)$ is complex differentiable, hence
continuous, on $\mathbb C\setminus\{p\}$ by
[[thm-algebra-of-complex-derivatives]] and
[[cor-complex-differentiability-implies-continuity]], the trace $\gamma^\ast$ is
contained in that set, and $\gamma$ is rectifiable, so
[[thm-existence-of-complex-line-integrals-on-rectifiable-paths]] applies.

Let $\gamma$ be a closed complex contour with trace $\gamma^\ast$ and length
$L(\gamma)$. Then $\mathbb C\setminus\gamma^\ast$ is open, and the index function
$p\mapsto n(\gamma,p)$ satisfies the quantitative estimate

$$|n(\gamma,p)-n(\gamma,p_0)|\ \le\ \frac{L(\gamma)\,|p-p_0|}{\pi\,d^2} \qquad\text{whenever }p_0\notin\gamma^\ast,\ d=\inf_{w\in\gamma^\ast}|w-p_0|,\ |p-p_0|<\tfrac d2 .$$

In particular $n(\gamma,\cdot)$ is continuous on $\mathbb C\setminus\gamma^\ast$;
it is constant on every connected component of that set; and since those
components are open, it is locally constant.

Let $\gamma$ be a closed complex contour with trace $\gamma^\ast$ and length
$L(\gamma)$. Then $\mathbb C\setminus\gamma^\ast$ has exactly one unbounded
connected component $U_\infty$, and

$$n(\gamma,p)=0\qquad\text{for every }p\in U_\infty.$$

More precisely, if $R>0$ satisfies $\gamma^\ast\subseteq\{z:|z|\le R\}$ and
$|p|>R+L(\gamma)/(2\pi)$, then $p\in U_\infty$ and $n(\gamma,p)=0$.

Let $\Gamma$ be an oriented closed piecewise-$C^1$ contour. Suppose that near $0$ it
contains exactly one regular $C^1$ arc, traversed once with positive real tangent, and
that the remaining contour is a compact set disjoint from $0$. Then for all sufficiently
small $\varepsilon>0$, the points $i\varepsilon$ and $-i\varepsilon$ avoid $\Gamma$ and
$n(\Gamma,i\varepsilon)-n(\Gamma,-i\varepsilon)=1$.

derivations.claim: Fix exterior points $q_1,q_2\notin P$ and choose $R>\max\{\max_{u\in P}\|u\|_2,\|q_1\|_2,\|q_2\|_2\}$, which exists because $P$ is compact. For each $j\in\{1,2\}$, compactness gives a nearest point $p_j\in P$. For every $u\in P$, convexity puts $p_j+t(u-p_j)$ in $P$ for $0\le t\le1$; minimality of $p_j$ gives $\|q_j-p_j\|_2^2\le\|q_j-p_j-t(u-p_j)\|_2^2$. Expanding, dividing by $t>0$, and letting $t\downarrow0$ yields $\langle q_j-p_j,u-p_j\rangle\le0$. Hence the ray $q_j+s(q_j-p_j)$, $s\ge0$, avoids $P$ and, being unbounded, meets the circle $C_R=\{w:|w|=R\}$. The circle $C_R$ is disjoint from $P$ and connected, so these two rays and an arc of $C_R$ join $q_1$ to $q_2$ in $\mathbb C\setminus P$. Thus $\mathbb C\setminus P$ is path-connected and unbounded.

By [F1], $n(\Gamma,q)$ is the winding index of the contour. Since $\Gamma\subset P$, the exterior $\mathbb C\setminus P$ lies in the unbounded component of $\mathbb C\setminus\Gamma$; [F3] gives $n(\Gamma,q)=0$ for every $q\notin P$.

Fix $z\in\operatorname{int}P$. Choose a ray from $z$ whose direction is not aimed at a vertex. Its intersection with the convex polygon is a bounded interval starting at $z$, so the ray exits at the interior $p$ of a single edge with directed tangent $v\ne0$. The polygon interior lies locally to the left of this positively oriented edge. Apply the orientation-preserving similarity $\rho(w)=\overline v(w-p)/|v|$, which sends $p$ to $0$ and the edge tangent to the positive real direction. For every $a\notin\Gamma$, put $c=\overline v/|v|$. Parametrizing the transformed contour and using [F1] gives $\int_{\rho\circ\Gamma}\frac{d\zeta}{\zeta-\rho(a)}=\int_\Gamma\frac{c\,dw}{c(w-a)}=\int_\Gamma\frac{dw}{w-a}$, so $n(\rho\circ\Gamma,\rho(a))=n(\Gamma,a)$. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, the points $\rho^{-1}(i\varepsilon)$ and $\rho^{-1}(-i\varepsilon)$ lie respectively on the interior and exterior local sides of the edge. Applying [F4] to $\rho\circ\Gamma$ gives $n(\rho\circ\Gamma,i\varepsilon)-n(\rho\circ\Gamma,-i\varepsilon)=1$; the just-proved invariance rewrites this as $n(\Gamma,\rho^{-1}(i\varepsilon))-n(\Gamma,\rho^{-1}(-i\varepsilon))=1$. The exterior-side index is zero by step 2.1. Thus an interior point near that edge has winding number one.

The interior of a convex polygon is connected. Its points avoid $\Gamma$, so [F2] makes the winding number constant throughout the interior. Step 3.1 identifies this constant as one. Together with step 2.1 this proves both cases.

Let $a<b$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^1$. Let $K\subseteq\Omega$ be compact and convex, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open. Assume that for every $s\in U$ the unique IVP solution $\phi(\cdot;s)$ from $\phi(a;s)=s$ exists on $[a,b]$ and $(t,\phi(t;s))\in K$ for every $t$. Then $s\mapsto\phi(t;s)$ is $C^1$ on $U$ for each $t\in[a,b]$. Its derivative matrix $S(t;s):=D_s\phi(t;s)$ is the unique solution of

$$S(t;s)=I_d+\int_a^t D_yf(r,\phi(r;s))S(r;s)\,dr,$$

and hence satisfies $\partial_tS=D_yf(t,\phi(t;s))S$, $S(a;s)=I_d$. The claim is local to the stated common compact tube; it does not assert differentiability beyond it.

Let U⊂R^n be open and Y:U→R^n be C¹. There is a unique maximal flow Φ on an open domain
D⊂R×U containing {0}×U, and Φ is jointly C¹. Its time slices are local C¹
diffeomorphisms with inverse Φ_{−t}; $\partial_t\Phi=Y(\Phi)$ and $D_p\Phi$ is the
unique solution V of $V′=DY(\Phi)V$, V(0)=I. Each regular point has a C¹ flow box. If Y
is C², Φ and those flow boxes are C²; the second state variation W satisfies
$W′=DY(\Phi)W+D²Y(\Phi)[Ve_i,Ve_j]$, W(0)=0. Individual trajectories of a C¹ field are
C² in time. A trajectory remaining in a compact K⊂⊂U cannot have a finite maximal
endpoint. These Euclidean conclusions use no full AC or DC.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For an autonomous vector field $\dot x=f(x)$, a nonconstant solution $x_*(t)$ with least positive period $T$ has periodic orbit $\Gamma=\{x_*(t):0\le t<T\}$. Its variational fundamental matrix $Y(t)$ solves

$$\dot Y(t)=D f(x_*(t))Y(t),\qquad Y(0)=I.$$

The matrix $Y(T)$ is the **monodromy matrix**; its eigenvalues, counted with algebraic multiplicity, are the **Floquet multipliers**. The multiplier $1$ in the direction $\dot x_*(0)$ is called the **phase multiplier**.

A **local Poincare section** at $x_*(0)$ is a smooth codimension-one surface through that point whose tangent space does not contain $f(x_*(0))$. The local return map sends a nearby point on the section to its next intersection after one turn around $\Gamma$. Its derivative at $x_*(0)$ is the Poincare derivative.

The orbit is **orbitally asymptotically stable** if it is Lyapunov stable as a set and the distance from every sufficiently nearby trajectory to $\Gamma$ tends to zero as time tends to $+\infty$. It is **orbitally unstable** if it is not Lyapunov stable as a set.

derivations.claim: Nonconstancy implies $f(x_*)\ne0$: otherwise the constant curve through $x_*$ is an IVP solution, and uniqueness in [F2] forces $\gamma$ to be that constant curve.

Differentiate the flow identity in [F2] with respect to $s$ at $s=0$. The chain rule [F3] gives $D_x\phi_T(x_*)f(x_*)$ on the left, while the time derivative on the right is $f(\phi_T(x_*))=f(x_*)$. By [F1] the left derivative is the monodromy action, hence $Mf(x_*)=f(x_*)$. Since $f(x_*)\ne0$ by step 1.1, this is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $1$, which is a Floquet multiplier by [F4].

Let $a<b$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^1$. Let $K\subseteq\Omega$ be compact and convex, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open. Assume that for every $s\in U$ the unique IVP solution $\phi(\cdot;s)$ from $\phi(a;s)=s$ exists on $[a,b]$ and $(t,\phi(t;s))\in K$ for every $t$. Then $s\mapsto\phi(t;s)$ is $C^1$ on $U$ for each $t\in[a,b]$. Its derivative matrix $S(t;s):=D_s\phi(t;s)$ is the unique solution of

$$S(t;s)=I_d+\int_a^t D_yf(r,\phi(r;s))S(r;s)\,dr,$$

and hence satisfies $\partial_tS=D_yf(t,\phi(t;s))S$, $S(a;s)=I_d$. The claim is local to the stated common compact tube; it does not assert differentiability beyond it.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $V:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a map. The
equation

$$x'(t)=V(x(t))$$

is an **autonomous ordinary differential equation**: its right-hand side depends
on the state alone and not explicitly on time. An initial value problem for this
equation consists of a time $t_0\in\mathbb R$ and a state $x_0\in U$, written
$x(t_0)=x_0$.

This is the special case of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]
obtained from the time-dependent field $F(t,x):=V(x)$ on
$\mathbb R\times U$. A solution on an interval $J$ is therefore a differentiable
curve $x:J\to U$ with $t_0\in J$ satisfying the equation at every $t\in J$ and
$x(t_0)=x_0$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Let $I=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a compact interval, let
$C:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be continuous, let $t_0\in I$, and let
$Y_0\in M_n(\mathbb R)$. Then the linear matrix initial value problem

$$Y'(t)=C(t)Y(t),\qquad Y(t_0)=Y_0,$$

has a unique solution on all of $I$.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: Fix a base state $x\in W$. By [F1], $\Phi$ is $C^1$ in $x$ and $S$ solves $S'=A S$, where $A(t)=Df(\Phi(t,x))$. The coefficient is bounded on $[0,T_+]$ by [F3]; integrating the variational equation by [F6] and applying [F5] bounds $S$ uniformly in $t$. The flow itself is jointly continuous in $(t,x)$ on the common tube by [F1] and the ODE relation [F2].

For a direction $h\in\mathbb R^n$, define a matrix $B_h(t)$ by $B_h(t)v=D^2f(\Phi(t,x))[S(t,x)h,S(t,x)v]$. It is continuous and has norm at most $C\|h\|_2$ for a finite constant $C$, by [F3] and the bound on $S$. Let $H_h$ solve $H_h'=AH_h+B_h$, $H_h(0)=0$. For each column, adjoining a constant coordinate turns its inhomogeneous linear IVP into a homogeneous linear system; applying [F4] to the augmented matrix gives a unique solution on $[0,T_+]$. Its integral equation from [F6] and [F5] give $\|H_h\|_\infty\le C'\|h\|_2$ for a finite constant $C'$.

For small $h$ with $x+h\in W$, put $\Delta(t)=\Phi(t,x+h)-\Phi(t,x)$, $S_h(t)=S(t,x+h)$, and $A_h(t)=Df(\Phi(t,x+h))$. The uniform remainder in [F1] gives $\Delta=S h+o(\|h\|_2)$ uniformly on $J$. On each segment between $\Phi(t,x)$ and $\Phi(t,x+h)$, the chain rule [F7] and [F6] applied coordinatewise to $Df$ give $ A_h-A=\int_0^1 D^2f(\Phi+s\Delta)[\Delta,\cdot] ds. $ Uniform continuity of $D^2f$ on $K$ [F3] and $\Delta=S h+o(\|h\|)$ therefore imply $A_h-A=D^2f(\Phi)[S h,\cdot]+o(\|h\|_2)$ uniformly in $t$.

The variational equations give $S_h'=A_hS_h$ and $S'=AS$. Subtract these and the equation for $H_h$ from step 2.1, setting $R_h=S_h-S-H_h$, to obtain $ R_h'=A_hR_h+(A_h-A)S+(A_h-A)H_h-B_h,\qquad R_h(0)=0. $ By step 2.2, $(A_h-A)S-B_h=o(\|h\|)$ uniformly; also $A_h-A=O(\|h\|)$ and $H_h=O(\|h\|)$ by steps 2.2 and 2.1. Thus the forcing after $A_hR_h$ is $o(\|h\|)$ uniformly. The coefficients $A_h$ are uniformly bounded on $K$, so [F5] applied to the integral equation for $R_h$ from [F6] gives $\|R_h\|_\infty=o(\|h\|_2)$. Therefore $D_xS(t,x)[h]=H_h(t)$, proving existence of the second state derivative.

If $x_j\to x$, [F1] gives uniform convergence of $\Phi(\cdot,x_j)$ and $S(\cdot,x_j)$ on $J$. Continuity of $D^2f$ on $K$ then gives uniform convergence of the coefficients and forcing in the linear equations for $H_h$; subtracting their integral equations and applying [F5] proves $H_h(\cdot,x_j)\to H_h(\cdot,x)$ uniformly. Thus the second state derivative is continuous in $(t,x)$.

By [F2], $\partial_t\Phi=f(\Phi)$. Differentiating this identity in $x$ and in $t$ using [F7] gives $\partial_{tx}\Phi=Df(\Phi)S$ and $\partial_{tt}\Phi=Df(\Phi)f(\Phi)$. These derivatives and $D_x^2\Phi=H$ are continuous by steps 1.1 and 4.1, so $\Phi$ is jointly $C^2$ on the stated tube.

Let $f:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be an autonomous $C^2$ vector field on an open set $U$, with the autonomous ODE convention of [[def-autonomous-ordinary-differential-equation]] and the $C^2$ map convention of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Let $\psi(x)=c^\top(x-x_{\rm ref})$ be an affine phase function with $c\ne0$. On the scaled interval $s\in[0,1]$, introduce the augmented state $u=(x,\theta)\in U\times(0,\infty)$ and vector field
$$
\widetilde f(x,\theta)=(\theta f(x),0).
$$
For endpoint states $u_0=(x_0,\theta_0)$ and $u_1=(x_1,\theta_1)$, define the boundary map
$$
B(u_0,u_1)=(x_1-x_0,\psi(x_0))\in\mathbb R^{d+1}.
$$
This is a square nonlinear BVP in the sense of [[def-nonlinear-two-point-bvp-and-boundary-residual]]: its state dimension and number of boundary equations are both $d+1$. The period coordinate is constant along solutions because its derivative is zero. The common-tube differentiability of the exact flow is given by [[lem-c1-ode-flow-on-common-tube]], and monodromy/Floquet terminology follows [[def-local-periodic-orbit-poincare-and-floquet-data]].

Whenever the exact autonomous flow $\phi_t$ exists on the required interval, the associated phase-bordered shooting residual is
$$
G(x,\theta)=\bigl(\phi_\theta(x)-x,\psi(x)\bigr)\in\mathbb R^{d+1},\qquad \theta>0.
$$
It is defined only for initial data whose flow exists through time $\theta$. Phase transversality at a nonstationary periodic point $x_*$ means $c^\top f(x_*)\ne0$. Neither existence of a zero nor invertibility of its Jacobian is part of this definition.

Fix $a<b$, an integer $d\ge1$, an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ containing $[a,b]\times$ the states under consideration, and a vector field $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$. Let $D_B\subseteq\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d$ be open and let $B:D_B\to\mathbb R^d$. A **square nonlinear two-point boundary-value problem (BVP)** is

$$y'(t)=f(t,y(t))\quad(a\le t\le b),\qquad B(y(a),y(b))=0,$$

Suppose $1$ is algebraically simple. Then [F4] implies that the complex eigenspace for eigenvalue $1$ is one-dimensional. By [F2] its spanning eigenvector $f_*$ is real, so the real kernel is $\mathbb R f_*$ and rank-nullity gives $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M-I_d)=d-1$. Choose a real basis $v_1,\ldots,v_{d-1}$ of $\operatorname{range}(M-I_d)$. The $d-1$ real linear forms $w\mapsto v_j^\top w$ are independent: if a linear combination vanishes for every $w$, then the row $\bigl(\sum_j a_jv_j\bigr)^\top$ is zero, so $\sum_j a_jv_j=0$ and basis independence forces every coefficient $a_j$ to vanish. Rank-nullity therefore gives a nonzero real $w_0$ with $v_j^\top w_0=0$ for every $j$. Thus $w_0^\top(M-I_d)=0$. It is a compatible left eigenvector with the real right eigenvector $f_*$, so [F3], applied over $\mathbb C$, gives $w_0^\top f_*\ne0$. This pairing is real; normalize $w=w_0/(w_0^\top f_*)$, so $w$ is real, $w^\top M=w^\top$, and $w^\top f_*=1$. For $Q=I-f_*w^\top$ and $W=\ker w^\top$, one has $Qf_*=0$, $Q|_W=I_W$, and $QM=M-f_*w^\top M=M-f_*w^\top=M-Mf_*w^\top=MQ$. Hence $Q$ is the projection onto $W$, $M$ preserves $W$, and $M-I_d$ maps $W$ into $W$. Its restriction to $W$ is injective: a kernel vector there would be an eigenvector independent of $f_*$, contrary to simplicity. Since $W$ is finite dimensional, [F7] makes the restriction invertible. For $J(u,\tau)=(r,s)$, left multiplication of the first row by $w^\top$ gives $\tau=w^\top r$. Write $u=u_W+\alpha f_*$ with $u_W\in W$; applying $Q$ to the first row and using its commutation with $M$ gives $u_W=((M-I_d)|_W)^{-1}Qr$, and the phase row gives $\alpha=(s-c^\top u_W)/(c^\top f_*)$. Thus nonzero $c^\top f_*$ gives a unique solution for every right-hand side, so $J$ is invertible. Moreover, $|\tau|\le\|w\|_2\|r\|_2$, $\|u_W\|_2\le K_W\|Q\|_2\|r\|_2$, and $|\alpha|\le(|s|+\|c\|_2K_W\|Q\|_2\|r\|_2)/|c^\top f_*|$. If $c^\top f_*=0$, then $J(f_*,0)=0$, so $J$ is singular. Now suppose the algebraic multiplicity of $1$ exceeds one. If the complex eigenspace has dimension at least two, its real kernel also has dimension at least two: for the real matrix $M-I_d$, its complex kernel consists exactly of $u+iv$ with $u$ and $v$ in the real kernel. Choose a real $v\in\ker(M-I_d)$ independent of $f_*$. $$G_{h,i}(Y)=\frac{Y_{i+1}-Y_i}{h}-f\!\left(t_i+\frac h2,\frac{Y_i+Y_{i+1}}2\right)\quad(0\le i<N),\qquad G_{h,N}(Y)=B(Y_0,Y_N).$$

symbol whenever $a \ge b$, and every additivity statement below would be
ill-formed as it is usually written. This item extends the notation, and nothing
else: the object it names is still the Darboux integral of
[[def-darboux-integral]].

Let $u, v \in \mathbb{R}$ and write

$$[u \wedge v,\ u \vee v] \;:=\; \text{the closed interval with endpoints } u \text{ and } v$$

([[def-interval]]). Let $f$ be a real-valued function whose domain contains that
interval. Say that **$f$ is integrable between $u$ and $v$** when either $u = v$,
or $u \ne v$ and the restriction of $f$ to $[u \wedge v,\ u \vee v]$ is bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux integrable there ([[def-darboux-integral]],
[[def-darboux-sums]]). For such $f$ define

$$\int_u^v f \;:=\; \begin{cases} \text{the Darboux integral of } f \text{ over } [u,v] & \text{if } u < v, \\[2pt] 0 & \text{if } u = v, \\[2pt] -\displaystyle\int_v^u f & \text{if } u > v. \end{cases}$$

**There is nothing to check for consistency.** The three clauses are indexed by
the three cases of trichotomy, $u < v$, $u = v$ and $u > v$, which are mutually
exclusive and exhaustive; no pair of them ever applies to the same $(u,v)$. In
particular the first clause is untouched, so on $u < v$ this is the published
integral verbatim and every published theorem about it applies unchanged.

**The middle clause is a stipulation, not a computation.** It is *not* claimed
that $0$ is a value forced by the $u < v$ definition in any limiting sense; that
definition simply says nothing at $u = v$, and $\int_u^u f := 0$ is what is
written there. It is also unconditional: no hypothesis on $f$ beyond being
defined at $u$ is asked for, since the case $u = v$ never refers to a partition.

### The two consequences used throughout the page

**Antisymmetry, for every pair.** For all reals $u, v$ with $f$ integrable
between them,

$$\int_u^v f \;=\; -\int_v^u f .$$

Indeed if $u < v$ then $v > u$ and the third clause reads
$\int_v^u f = -\int_u^v f$, which rearranges to the display; if $u = v$ both
sides are $0$; and if $u > v$ the third clause is the display itself.

**Absolute values agree.** Consequently
$\bigl|\int_u^v f\bigr| = \bigl|\int_v^u f\bigr|$ for every such pair.

**An obligation recorded here and discharged elsewhere.** With this convention
the additivity identity

$$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f$$

holds for **every** arrangement of $u, v, w$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable, not only for $u < v < w$. That is a theorem and not part of this
definition; it is proved as the last clause of
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], and nothing on this page uses it before it
is proved there.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be Banach spaces over the same scalar field
([[def-banach-space]]).

1. If $R\in\mathcal B(X)$ satisfies $\|R\|<1$
   ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-operator-norm]]), then $I-R$ is
   invertible with inverse the operator-norm limit of the partial sums
   $\sum_{n<N}R^n$, the norm limit being taken in
   $\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]), and
   $$\Bigl\|\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}R^n\Bigr\|\le\frac{1}{1-\|R\|}.$$
2. If $A\in\mathcal B(X,Y)$ is invertible with $A^{-1}\in\mathcal B(Y,X)$ and
   $E\in\mathcal B(X,Y)$ satisfies $\|A^{-1}E\|<1$, then $A+E$ is invertible
   with $(A+E)^{-1}=\bigl(I+A^{-1}E\bigr)^{-1}A^{-1}\in\mathcal B(Y,X)$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

B(u_0,u_1)=(x_1-x_0,\psi(x_0))\in\mathbb R^{d+1}.

Whenever the exact autonomous flow $\phi_t$ exists on the required interval, the associated phase-bordered shooting residual is
$$
G(x,\theta)=\bigl(\phi_\theta(x)-x,\psi(x)\bigr)\in\mathbb R^{d+1},\qquad \theta>0.
$$
It is defined only for initial data whose flow exists through time $\theta$. Phase transversality at a nonstationary periodic point $x_*$ means $c^\top f(x_*)\ne0$. Neither existence of a zero nor invertibility of its Jacobian is part of this definition.

At a phase-fixed periodic point $x_*$ with period $T$, let $M=D_x\phi_T(x_*)$, let $f_*=f(x_*)\ne0$, and let $c=D\psi(x_*)$ for the affine phase $\psi(x)=c^\top(x-x_{\rm ref})$. The derivative of the phase-bordered shooting residual is
$$ J=\begin{bmatrix}M-I_d&f_*\\c^\top&0\end{bmatrix}. $$
It is invertible if and only if $1$ is an algebraically simple eigenvalue of $M$ and $c^\top f_*\ne0$. Let $\lambda$ be a simple eigenvalue of $A$, and let $x,y\ne0$ be compatible
right and left eigenvectors. Then $y^\ast x\ne0$. Consequently, after rescaling
either vector, one may impose the normalization

$$y^\ast x=1.$$

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, equipped with the standard Hermitian inner
product, and let $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ be a simple eigenvalue of $A$. A nonzero vector
$x$ is a **right eigenvector** for $\lambda$ if

$$Ax=\lambda x.$$

A nonzero vector $y$ is a **left eigenvector** for $\lambda$ if

$$y^\ast A=\lambda y^\ast,$$

equivalently $A^\ast y=\overline{\lambda}\,y$.

Such $x$ and $y$ are called **compatible left and right eigenvectors** for the
simple eigenvalue $\lambda$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

An endomorphism of a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space has a Jordan canonical form over $F$ if and only if its characteristic polynomial splits into linear factors over $F$. This includes the zero space, where the characteristic polynomial is $1$ and the Jordan form is empty.

differentiable compatible eigenvectors $x(t),y(t)$ normalized by

For an autonomous vector field $\dot x=f(x)$, a nonconstant solution $x_*(t)$ with least positive period $T$ has periodic orbit $\Gamma=\{x_*(t):0\le t<T\}$. Its variational fundamental matrix $Y(t)$ solves

$$\dot Y(t)=D f(x_*(t))Y(t),\qquad Y(0)=I.$$

The matrix $Y(T)$ is the **monodromy matrix**; its eigenvalues, counted with algebraic multiplicity, are the **Floquet multipliers**. The multiplier $1$ in the direction $\dot x_*(0)$ is called the **phase multiplier**.

A **local Poincare section** at $x_*(0)$ is a smooth codimension-one surface through that point whose tangent space does not contain $f(x_*(0))$. The local return map sends a nearby point on the section to its next intersection after one turn around $\Gamma$. Its derivative at $x_*(0)$ is the Poincare derivative.

The orbit is **orbitally asymptotically stable** if it is Lyapunov stable as a set and the distance from every sufficiently nearby trajectory to $\Gamma$ tends to zero as time tends to $+\infty$. It is **orbitally unstable** if it is not Lyapunov stable as a set.

For each fixed $\mu$, let $\Phi_\theta(q)$ be the time-$\theta$ flow of $q'=g(q)$, so its parameter coordinates remain constant. For an affine phase $\psi(x)=c^\top(x-x_{\rm ref})$, define
$$
G(q,\theta)=\begin{bmatrix}P\Phi_\theta(q)-Pq\\\psi(Pq)\end{bmatrix}.
$$
For $p=0$ this is the shooting residual in [[def-phase-bordered-periodic-orbit-bvp]]. Its Jacobian is
$$
DG(q,\theta)=\begin{bmatrix}P\mathcal M-P& f(P\Phi_\theta(q),\mu)\\ c^\top P&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad \mathcal M=D_q\Phi_\theta(q).
$$

To enclose the period column, let $X_T$ be the first $d$ coordinate projection of the successful endpoint enclosure $Y_N$. The exact augmented endpoint lies in $X_T\times\Lambda$: its parameter equals its initial value in $\Lambda$, even if a returned interval coordinate is wider. Let $\lambda\in D$ be an eigenvalue of $A+E$ with eigenvector $x=\alpha v+y$, $y\in W$. If $\alpha=0$, projection onto $W$ gives $y=(\lambda I_W-A_W)^{-1}QE y$. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $f$ be meromorphic on $\Omega$, and
let $\Gamma$ be admissible for the residue theorem in $\Omega$. Suppose in
addition that $f$ is not identically zero on any connected component of
$\Omega$ and that $f(z)\ne0$ for every $z\in\Gamma^\ast$. Then

$$\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma \frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}\,dz=Z(f,\Gamma)-P(f,\Gamma),$$

where the weighted zero and pole counts are those of
[[def-weighted-zero-and-pole-counts-on-cycle]].

Only finitely many terms in those weighted counts are nonzero.

Let $v_0,\ldots,v_{m-1}\in\mathbb Q+i\mathbb Q$, $m\ge3$, be the cyclically ordered vertices of a simple strictly convex polygon whose edges are traversed counterclockwise. Let $P$ be its filled convex hull and let $\Gamma$ be the concatenation of its oriented edges. For every $z\notin\Gamma$, the winding number $n(\Gamma,z)$ is $1$ if $z\in\operatorname{int}P$ and $0$ if $z\notin P$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

Let $f \in \mathbb C[x]$ have degree $n \ge 1$. Then there exist distinct
complex numbers $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$ and positive integers
$m_1,\dots,m_r$ such that
$$ f(x)=c\prod_{j=1}^r (x-\alpha_j)^{m_j} $$
for some $c \in \mathbb C^\times$, with
$$ m_1+\cdots+m_r=n. $$
These exponents are uniquely determined by $f$. Equivalently, $f$ has exactly
$n$ roots counted with multiplicity.

For every $x\in\mathbb R$,

$$\frac{d}{dx}\arctan x=\frac1{1+x^2},\qquad \arctan x=\int_0^x\frac{dt}{1+t^2}.$$

For $|x|<1$,

$$\arctan x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n x^{2n+1}}{2n+1}.$$

At the endpoint, the ordinarily convergent alternating series satisfies

$$\frac\pi4=1-\frac13+\frac15-\frac17+\cdots.$$

Let $(\varepsilon_k)$ be the alternating sequence of [[lem-alternating-sequence]],
that is the unique sequence of reals with $\varepsilon_0 = 1$ and
$\varepsilon_{k+1} = -\varepsilon_k$, which is what is usually written
$\varepsilon_k = (-1)^k$; let $e$ and $o$ be its even and odd index maps, so that
$\varepsilon_{e_j} = 1$, $\varepsilon_{o_j} = -1$, and every natural number is
$e_j$ for exactly one $j$ or $o_j$ for exactly one $j$.

Let $(b_k)$ be a sequence of reals that is nonincreasing
([[def-monotone-sequence]]) and converges to $0$ ([[def-real-limit]]); then
$b_k \ge 0$ for every $k$. Write $t_n := \sum_{k<n} \varepsilon_k b_k$ for the
partial sums ([[def-series]]). Then:

1. the series $\sum \varepsilon_k b_k$ converges; write $L$ for its sum;
2. $t_{e_j} \le L \le t_{o_j}$ for every $j \in \mathbb{N}$, and for every

3. $|L - t_n| \le b_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Claim 3 is the error bound: the partial sum $t_n$, which uses the $n$ terms
$\varepsilon_0 b_0, \dots, \varepsilon_{n-1}b_{n-1}$, differs from the sum by at

**Only claim 1 is a corollary of [[thm-dirichlet-test]].** Claims 2 and 3 are not:
they come from the interlacing of the even-index and odd-index partial sums, and

Input a positive integer $n$, a nonempty complex matrix family $\mathcal M$ enclosed entrywise by finite dyadic real/imaginary rectangles, a dyadic center matrix $M_0$, a certified dyadic bound $\delta_A\ge\sup_{M\in\mathcal M}\|M-M_0\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}$, and a simple positively oriented strictly convex polygon $\Gamma$ with dyadic vertices and filled interior $P$. Supply the dyadic disk cover and point preconditioners required by [[alg-complex-resolvent-cover-validator]], a positive integer $N$ for midpoint subdivisions of each edge, a positive integer $K_\pi$ for the arctangent series, and a finite arithmetic budget. The family may be the monodromy block of a validated shooting jet; no correlation between matrix entries is required. A complex rectangle here is the product of one closed dyadic real interval and one closed dyadic imaginary interval for each matrix entry.

1. Verify the polygon orientation/strict convexity exactly, then run the resolvent-cover validator on every edge for the entire family. If any segment is uncovered, an outward inequality is not strict, or no finite upper bound $m$ on $\|(zI-M)^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}$ is returned, output `inconclusive`.
2. Subdivide each oriented edge $e_j=b_j-a_j$ into $N$ equal parts, with rational midpoints $z_{jk}=a_j+(k+1/2)e_j/N$. By exact rational complex elimination, compute $R^0_{jk}=(z_{jk}I-M_0)^{-1}$; a singular center matrix or an incomplete operation returns `inconclusive`. For each rational complex entry $a+ib$ of $R^0_{jk}$, use rational square-root bisection to find an upper bound for $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$, then sum row bounds to obtain $b_{jk}\ge\|R^0_{jk}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}$. Use the same bisection to obtain $s_j\ge|e_j|$. If the finite budget does not produce these rational bounds, return `inconclusive`.
3. Form the exact center midpoint sum
$$S_0=\sum_j\frac{e_j}{N}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\operatorname{tr}R^0_{jk},$$
and the outward error allowance
$$E=\frac{n m^2}{2N}\sum_j|e_j|^2+\frac{n m\delta_A}{N}\sum_{j,k}s_jb_{jk}.$$
The first term uses the exact rational squared modulus of each rational edge; the second uses the rational upper edge length $s_j$. The first term bounds midpoint quadrature error; the second bounds replacing each family resolvent by the center resolvent. All sums and products are exact rationals; if a required rational square-root upper bound is unavailable, return `inconclusive`.
4. Enclose $\pi$ using $\pi=4\arctan(1)$ and the alternating partial sum $4\sum_{k=0}^{K_\pi-1}(-1)^k/(2k+1)$ with tail radius $4/(2K_\pi+1)$. Require a positive lower endpoint. Using exact rational endpoint arithmetic, enclose $S_0/(2\pi i)$ and inflate its real and imaginary intervals by $E/(2\pi_{\rm low})$; call the resulting rectangle $I$.
5. Choose an integer $c$ and return `certified-count(c)` only if $0\le c\le n$, $\operatorname{Re}I\subset(c-1/2,c+1/2)$, $\operatorname{Im}I\subset(-1/2,1/2)$, and $0\in\operatorname{Im}I$. The root multiplicities are those of the characteristic polynomial by [[thm-complex-polynomial-has-exactly-degree-many-roots-counted-with-multiplicity]]. The rational $\pi$ enclosure uses [[thm-principal-inverse-tangent-calculus]] and [[thm-alternating-series-test]].

Since each diagonal entry is bounded by its row sum, $|\operatorname{tr}A|\le n\|A\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}$, so [F1] and [F7] give $|g\prime(t)|\le n|e|^2m^2$. Form the outward interval box
$$
K=x_0-CF_0+(I-CJ(Y))(Y-x_0).
$$
Every root of $F$ in $Y$ lies in $K$. Thus $K\cap Y=\varnothing$ proves that $Y$ has no root. If $K\subset\operatorname{int}Y$, then $F$ has at least one root in $Y$. Define $\|v\|_\infty=\max_i|v_i|$ and $\|A\|_\infty=\max_i\sum_j|A_{ij}|$. Let $E$ be the outward interval matrix enclosing $I-CJ(Y)$ and put $\bar q=\max_i\sum_j\max(|\inf E_{ij}|,|\sup E_{ij}|)$. If $\bar q<1$, then $F$ has at most one root in $Y$; strict inclusion together with this bound proves a unique root. No uniqueness is inferred from strict inclusion alone.

For an autonomous vector field $\dot x=f(x)$, a nonconstant solution $x_*(t)$ with least positive period $T$ has periodic orbit $\Gamma=\{x_*(t):0\le t<T\}$. Its variational fundamental matrix $Y(t)$ solves

$$\dot Y(t)=D f(x_*(t))Y(t),\qquad Y(0)=I.$$

The matrix $Y(T)$ is the **monodromy matrix**; its eigenvalues, counted with algebraic multiplicity, are the **Floquet multipliers**. The multiplier $1$ in the direction $\dot x_*(0)$ is called the **phase multiplier**.

A **local Poincare section** at $x_*(0)$ is a smooth codimension-one surface through that point whose tangent space does not contain $f(x_*(0))$. The local return map sends a nearby point on the section to its next intersection after one turn around $\Gamma$. Its derivative at $x_*(0)$ is the Poincare derivative.

The orbit is **orbitally asymptotically stable** if it is Lyapunov stable as a set and the distance from every sufficiently nearby trajectory to $\Gamma$ tends to zero as time tends to $+\infty$. It is **orbitally unstable** if it is not Lyapunov stable as a set.

$$
B(u_0,u_1)=(x_1-x_0,\psi(x_0))\in\mathbb R^{d+1}.

Differentiating $r(1-r)$ at $r=1$ gives the radial variational equation $\dot\rho=-\rho$, whose multiplier is $e^{-2\pi}<1$; the angular variational equation is $\dot\alpha=0$, whose multiplier is $1$.
